edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De corona militis, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Proxime facta est liberalitas praestantissimorum imperatorum; expungebantur in castris milites laureati. Adhibetur quidam illic magis Dei miles, caeteris constantior fratribus, qui se duobus dominis servire posse praesumpserant, solus libero eapite, coronamento in manu otioso. Vulgata jam et ista disciplina Christianorum relucebat. Denique singuli designare, et eludere eminus, infrendere cominus. Murmur tribuno defertur, et persona jam ex ordine accesserat. Statim tribunus: Cur, inquit, tam diversus habitu? Negavit ille cum caeteris sibi licere; caussas expostulatus, Christianus sum, respondit. O militem in Deo gloriosum! Suffragia exinde, et res ampliata, et reus ad praefectos. Ibidem gravissimas penulas posuit, relevari auspicatus, speculatoriam morosissimam de pedibus absolvit, terrae sanctae insistere incipiens, gladium nec dominicae defensioni necessarium reddidit: laurea et de manu corruit. Et nunc russatus sanguinis sui spe, calceatus de Evangelii paratura, succinctus acutiore verbo Dei, totus de Apostolo armatus et de martyrii candida melius coronandus, donativum Christi in carcere exspectat. Exinde sententiae super illo, nescio an Christianorum, non enim aliae ethnicorum, ut de abrupto, et praecipiti, et mori cupido, qui de habitu interrogatus nomini negotium fecerit: solus scilicet fortis, inter tot fratres commilitones solus Christianus. Plane superest ut etiam martyria recusare meditentur, qui prophetias ejusdem Spiritus sancti respuerunt. Mussitant denique, tam bonam et longam sibi pacem periclitari. Nec dubito quosdam Scripturas emigrare, sarcinas expedire, fugae accingi de civitate in civitatem; nullam enim aliam Evangelii memoriam curant. Novi et pastores corum, in pace leones, in praelio cervos. Sed de quaestionibus confessionum alibi docebimus. At nunc quatenus et illud opponunt: Ubi autem prohibemur coronari? Hanc magis localem substantiam caussae praesentis aggrediar, ut et qui ex sollicitudine ignorantiae quaerunt, instruantur; et qui in defensionem delicti contendunt, revincantur; ipsi vel maxime Christiani laureati, quibus id solum quaestio est; quasi aut nullum aut incertum saltem haberi possit delictum quod patiatur quaestionem. Nec nullum autem nec incertum, hinc interim ostendam.
thought_title: The Christian and the Laurel Wreath
pass_a_gloss: Recently there was a generosity of the most excellent emperors; the soldiers who were crowned were being discharged from the camp. A certain soldier of God was present there, more steadfast than the other brothers, who had presumed that he could serve two lords, alone with a free head, with a laurel wreath idle in his hand. Now this discipline of the Christians was already well-known. Finally, the individuals began to point him out and to mock him from a distance and to sneer at him up close. A murmur was reported to the tribune, and the person had already stepped forward in order. Immediately the tribune said: Why are you so different in appearance? He denied that it was permitted to him along with the others; when he was asked for a reason, he responded: I am a Christian. O glorious soldier in God! From then on, there were votes and the matter was enlarged, and the defendant was brought before the prefects. There he put on the most serious penalties, having dared to be relieved, he released the most sluggish watch from his feet, beginning to insist on the holy ground, he did not render the sword necessary for the Lord's defense: the laurel wreath also fell from his hand. And now, having been spattered with the hope of his own blood, shod with the preparation of the Gospel, girded with the sharper word of God, entirely armed with the Apostle and better crowned with the white of martyrdom, he awaits the gift of Christ in prison. From then on, the opinions about him, I do not know whether of the Christians, for certainly not of the others of the gentiles, as if from a precipice, and steep, and desiring to die, who having been asked about his appearance made a business of the name: alone certainly strong, among so many brothers and fellow soldiers alone a Christian. It remains, of course, that they also intend to refuse martyrdom, who have rejected the prophecies of the same Holy Spirit. They murmur, finally, that such a good and long peace is being endangered for them. And I do not doubt that some of them will migrate, pack their bags, prepare for flight from city to city; for they do not care about any other memory of the Gospel. And I know their shepherds, lions in peace, deer in battle. But we will teach about the questions of confessions elsewhere. Now, however, as far as they also object: But where are we forbidden to be crowned? I will attack this more local substance of the present cause, so that both those who ask out of anxious ignorance may be instructed, and those who strive in defense of the offense may be overcome; especially the Christian laureates themselves, for whom this is the only question; as if there could be no offense or at least an uncertain one that would allow a question. And I will show that it is neither none nor uncertain, at least for now.
pass_b_english: The most excellent emperors had just staged a largesse; crowned soldiers were being discharged from camp. A certain soldier of God stood there, more steadfast than the rest of the brothers, men who had presumed they could serve two masters — he alone, bareheaded, with a laurel wreath idle in his hand. By now the Christians' discipline was notorious. Soon individuals began singling him out, mocking him from a distance, sneering up close. A murmur reached the tribune, and the man had already stepped forward in ranks. The tribune demanded at once, "Why do you look so different?" He denied that what the others did was permitted to him; pressed for a reason, he answered, "I am a Christian." O glorious soldier in God! From then on votes were cast, the case escalated, and the defendant was hauled before the prefects. There he accepted the harshest penalties, seeking discharge; he cast off the sluggish watch from his feet, planted himself on holy ground, refused to treat the sword as necessary for the Lord's defense, and the laurel fell from his hand as well. And now, spattered with the hope of his own blood, shod with the Gospel's preparation, girded with the sharper word of God, fully armed with the Apostle and better crowned with the white of martyrdom, he awaits Christ's gift in prison. Afterward came the verdicts on him — I do not know whether from Christians, for certainly not from the gentiles — as if from a sheer precipice, steep and death-desiring, that a man questioned about his uniform should make an issue of the Name: alone, truly strong, among so many brother comrades-in-arms, alone a Christian. It follows, of course, that those who have spat on the prophecies of the same Holy Spirit now intend to refuse martyrdom as well. They whisper at the end that such a good and long peace is being endangered for them. And I do not doubt some will migrate, pack their bags, prepare flight from city to city; for they care for no other memory of the Gospel. I know their shepherds too: lions in peace, deer in battle. But we will teach on the questions of confessions elsewhere. Now, however, as far as they also object: "Where are we forbidden to be crowned?" I will tackle this concrete core of the present case, so that both those who ask from anxious ignorance may be instructed and those who strive to defend the offense may be confuted — especially the Christian laureates themselves, for whom this is the only question; as if there could be no offense, or at least an uncertain one, that would admit debate. It is neither non-existent nor uncertain, and I will show that, at least for now.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent, accurate rendering that preserves all nuances of agency, negation, and modality. The translation of 'solus libero eapite' as 'alone with a free head' (A) and 'he alone, bareheaded' (B) correctly interprets the sense of the Latin. The complex sentence regarding the 'opinions' (sententiae) is handled well in both. No omissions or contradictions found.
